sermon:
## Order in the House, Silence to the Liars
*What a church builds when it builds with proven men, and what it loses when it doesn't*

**Text:** Titus 1 · **Supporting:** 1 Timothy 3:1-7 · Acts 20:29-30 · 2 Timothy 4:3-4 · Matthew 7:16

Paul did not leave Crete because the work was finished. He left it because the work was barely started, and he left it in the hands of one man with a hard assignment. "This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you." (Titus 1:5) Put what remained into order. The church on Crete was not a building or a budget. It was a scattering of new believers in towns full of false teachers, and the only thing standing between those believers and ruin was whether qualified men would be appointed to lead them. We have built churches on every other foundation. We have built on the gifted, the charismatic, the available, the willing. Paul builds on the proven.

**The list is the love.**
We read the qualifications and we hear a checklist, and a checklist feels cold, bureaucratic, like an application for a job no one wants. But read what Paul actually requires. "If anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination." (Titus 1:6) Then the longer list: "For an overseer, as God's steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined." (Titus 1:7-8) Notice what is almost entirely absent. There is one line about ability — "He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught" (Titus 1:9) — and the rest is character. Not eloquence. Not strategy. Not the size of the crowd he can gather. Whether he is arrogant. Whether he loses his temper. Whether he drinks. Whether he is greedy. Paul is describing a man you could trust with your daughter, your money, and your soul, and he is saying that this and nothing less is what a church requires at its head. The same standard runs through 1 Timothy 3, where Paul tells a different church the same thing: the overseer must be "above reproach," must "manage his own household well," must "not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit." The pattern does not change from one city to the next, because the danger does not change. A church gets the leaders it appoints, and it becomes what its leaders are.

**The empty talk that ruins houses.**
Then Paul turns, and the temperature rises, because the reason character matters so much is that the alternative is already inside the door. "For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach." (Titus 1:10-11) Upsetting whole families. Not annoying a few people. Overturning households — marriages, children, the faith of an entire family — for shameful gain. This is the thing Paul saw coming years before, when he gathered the Ephesian elders and told them, "I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them." From among your own selves. The threat is never only out there. It rises from inside the leadership of the church, from men who learned the language and kept the ambition, and the only defense Paul names is elders who hold firm to the word and are strong enough to silence the liars. Paul even quotes the Cretans' own poet against them — "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons" (Titus 1:12) — not to insult a culture, but to say the soil is real and the weeds are real and pretending otherwise is how the weeds win.

**You are the watching family.**
Here is where I stop describing Crete. Because I have wanted the gifted man more than the godly one. I have sat in rooms — I have run rooms — where the question was whether someone could draw a crowd, and the question of whether he was quick-tempered or greedy got folded in quietly at the end, if it got asked at all. We have built the modern church on a platform and then wondered why it keeps collapsing under the men we put on it. Paul tells us why. We appointed competence and called it calling. The fruit tells the truth, every time. "You will recognize them by their fruits," Jesus said. "Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles?" The test is not the sermon. The test is the home, the temper, the money, the marriage — the life no one sees from the third row. And the mercy in this hard chapter is that the standard was first met by One. Before any elder was qualified, the great Shepherd was qualified — above reproach, never arrogant, never grasping for gain, who emptied himself and gave himself for the very flock the wolves came to scatter. The grace of God appeared in him, and it does not appoint us and leave us as it found us. It purifies a people of his own possession, and then it sets proven men over them to guard what it purchased. A church without that guard is a church with the door open and the wolves already counting the houses.

Character qualifies. Empty talk must stop.

## The Doctrine That Adorns
*How right teaching shows up in an ordinary life, and the grace that makes it possible*

**Text:** Titus 2 · **Supporting:** Titus 2:11-14 · Ephesians 2:8-10 · 1 Peter 2:12 · Romans 6:1-2

There is a sentence at the hinge of this chapter that should stop us. Paul has just told the older men to be sober-minded, the older women to teach what is good, the young women to love their husbands and children, the young men to be self-controlled, the slaves to be trustworthy — an ordinary list of ordinary people doing ordinary good — and then he says why. "So that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior." (Titus 2:10) Adorn the doctrine. The word is the one you would use for setting a jewel, for arranging something so that its beauty is finally seen. Paul is telling a slave that the way he does his work can make the truth about God beautiful to the people watching. We have separated doctrine and life as though one were for the mind and the other for Monday. Paul welds them. The teaching is shown in the living, or it is not believed at all.

**Sound doctrine has a shape, and the shape is a person.**
Notice that Paul never gives Titus a doctrinal lecture to deliver. He gives him people to teach and a way for them to live. "But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine." (Titus 2:1) What accords with sound doctrine — not the doctrine itself first, but the life that fits it, the way a garment fits the body it was cut for. Older men, sober and steadfast. Older women, reverent, not slanderers, teaching the younger. Young women, loving their families. Young men, self-controlled, with Titus himself "a model of good works" (Titus 2:7) so that any opponent "may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us" (Titus 2:8). Every category. Every age. Every station, down to the household slave with no power and no platform. Sound doctrine is not an idea reserved for the educated. It is a way of being that reaches the person with the least, and Peter says the watching pagan world is the audience: "Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God." The neighbor does not read your theology. He reads your life and concludes something about your God. This is why Paul ranges across every category and leaves no one out. The old man cannot say he is past the work of self-control; the young woman cannot say her marriage and her home are too small to matter; the slave cannot say he has no platform and therefore no witness. Each one, in his station, sets the jewel of the doctrine or smudges it. There is no neutral life. The truth about God is being either adorned or obscured in your kitchen, your office, your temper, today.

**Grace teaches. That is the engine of the whole chapter.**
Then Paul tells us where any of this comes from, and it is not from trying harder. "For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age." (Titus 2:11-12) Read that again slowly, because it overturns what most of us were taught. Grace appeared. Grace saves. And then grace trains. The same grace that pardons is the grace that schools, and it schools us to say no — to renounce, to refuse, to put down the ungodliness and the worldly passions we had made our home in. Grace is not the soft permission to stay as we are. Grace is the strong teacher that will not leave us as we are. This is the answer to the oldest objection against the gospel, the one Paul names in Romans: "Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means." The person who thinks grace means sin no longer matters has never met this grace. Real grace says no through us. It gets into the temper, the appetite, the marriage, the wallet — the same places the elder was tested in chapter one — and it begins to train them. Not by law applied from outside. By grace appearing from inside.

**You are being trained, and you are waiting for a face.**
I have used grace as a permission slip. I have preached forgiveness and quietly meant by it that nothing had to change, that the cross had bought me the right to stay exactly as comfortable and unconfronted as I was, and I have done it from a pulpit. That is not the grace of Titus 2. The grace of Titus 2 saves a man and then sits him down and teaches him to say no to the very things he loved, and it does this while he is "waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." (Titus 2:13) That is the whole posture of the trained life — between two appearings. Grace appeared once, in a manger and on a cross, and grace will appear again in glory, and we live the whole stretch between as people who have seen the first and are waiting on the second. And Paul tells us exactly what that first appearing did: he "gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works." (Titus 2:14) He did not redeem us to leave us lawless and call it freedom. He purified a people for himself. The good works are not the price of belonging to him. They are the proof that he has done what he came to do. He gave himself for us. The only fitting answer is a life that adorns it.

Grace teaches us to say no.

## Saved by Mercy, Ready for Good
*Why the people God rescued by no merit of their own become the people most ready to serve*

**Text:** Titus 3 · **Supporting:** Titus 3:3-7 · Ephesians 2:8-10 · John 3:5 · 2 Timothy 2:23-24

Paul ends the letter the way he began it — with ordinary life — and it is easy to miss how radical the opening instruction is. "Be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people." (Titus 3:1-2) Toward all people. Not toward the deserving. Not toward the agreeable. Toward all — including the rulers of Crete, the false teachers, the neighbors who slandered them. We treat gentleness as something we extend to people once they have earned it. Paul treats it as something the gospel owes to everyone, and then he tells us why, and the why is the heart of the letter.

**Remember what you were.**
"For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another." (Titus 3:3) We ourselves. Not them — us. Paul will not let Titus stand over the foolish and the disobedient, because Paul will not stand over them either. He puts himself in the list. Slaves to passions. Passing our days in malice and envy. Hating one another. That is the autobiography of every person before grace, and it is the only honest ground for gentleness toward all. You cannot look down on the people you were five years from joining. The man who remembers what he was rescued from does not sneer at the man still drowning. He remembers the hand that reached for him, and he reaches.

**But God.**
Then comes the great reversal of the whole New Testament, the two words on which everything turns. "But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life." (Titus 3:4-7) Stop on the engine of that sentence. Not because of works done by us in righteousness. According to his own mercy. We were not the kind of people God should have saved, and we did not become that kind of people first and then get saved. He saved us in our foolishness, in our malice, mid-drowning, on the strength of nothing in us and everything in him. This is what Paul means everywhere: "By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast." The washing of regeneration is the new birth Jesus told Nicodemus no man could arrange for himself — "unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." You did not wash yourself. You were washed. And it was poured out "richly" — not measured, not rationed to match what you brought, because you brought nothing. The mercy is lavish precisely because it is mercy and not wages. A wage is calculated. Mercy is poured.

**Saved by no works, now ready for every one.**
Here is the turn, and I have gotten it backward most of my life. If God saved us by mercy and not by works, the lazy conclusion is that works no longer matter — that grace has retired us. Paul concludes the exact opposite. "The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works." (Titus 3:8) Devote themselves. Be careful to. The people saved entirely apart from their works are the people Paul most insists must be ready for every good work — because the same Ephesians sentence that says "not a result of works" finishes, "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works." Not saved by them. Saved for them. And then Paul, with the whole weight of this mercy behind him, tells Titus to be done with the thing that wastes it: "Avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless." (Titus 3:9) I have spent hours I will not get back winning arguments that profited no one — defending the truth in a tone that denied it, contending for the gospel as though I had earned it rather than been handed it bleeding and undeserving. The Lord's servant, Paul tells Timothy, "must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone." There is a kind of fighting that looks like faithfulness and is only pride wearing doctrine as armor, and Paul names it worthless to its face. The man who knows he was saved by sheer mercy has nothing to prove and everyone to serve. He was foolish, and he was washed. He brought nothing, and he was made an heir. So he speaks evil of no one, he is gentle toward all, and he gets to work — not to be saved, but because he already is. The grace that appeared did not leave him idle. It made him ready.

He saved us. Now be ready.
